name.text: PHYSICS_MCQI_KINETICTHEORY_MCQ_Q01 - Pressure of ideal gas in moving rocket

questiontext.text: 13.1 A cubic vessel (with faces horizontal + vertical) contains an ideal gas at NTP. The vessel is being carried by a rocket which is moving at a speed of \(500\text{ m s}^{-1}\) in vertical direction. The pressure of the gas inside the vessel as observed by us on the ground

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to the kinetic theory of gases, the pressure exerted by an ideal gas on the walls of its container arises from the rate of change of momentum of the gas molecules colliding with the walls, which depends on the velocity of the gas molecules relative to the walls of the container.

Step 2: Evaluation
When the rocket moves at a constant vertical speed of \(500\text{ m s}^{-1}\), the entire cubic vessel and the ideal gas molecules inside it move together with the same bulk velocity of \(500\text{ m s}^{-1}\). Because both the container walls and the gas molecules share this uniform translational motion, the relative velocity of the molecules with respect to the walls remains completely unchanged.

Step 3: Application
Since the relative motion between the gas molecules and the vessel walls is unaffected, the frequency of collisions and the momentum transferred per collision to every face (top, bottom, and vertical faces) remain identical to their values when the vessel is at rest. Moreover, pressure is a frame-independent scalar quantity under Galilean transformations for a gas in a closed moving vessel.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The pressure of the gas inside the vessel as observed from the ground remains the same because the motion of the vessel as a whole does not affect the relative motion of the gas molecules and the walls.

answer.text: remains the same because \(500\text{ m s}^{-1}\) is very much smaller than \(v_{\text{rms}}\) of the gas.
remains the same because motion of the vessel as a whole does not affect the relative motion of the gas molecules and the walls.
will increase by a factor equal to \(\frac{v_{\text{rms}}^2 + (500)^2}{v_{\text{rms}}^2}\) where \(v_{\text{rms}}\) was the original mean square velocity of the gas.
will be different on the top wall and bottom wall of the vessel.

name.text: PHYSICS_MCQI_KINETICTHEORY_MCQ_Q02 - Pressure on totally absorbing cube face

questiontext.text: 13.2 1 mole of an ideal gas is contained in a cubical volume \(V\), \(\text{ABCDEFGH}\) at \(300\text{ K}\) (Fig. 13.1). One face of the cube (\(\text{EFGH}\)) is made up of a material which totally absorbs any gas molecule incident on it. At any given time,

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
One mole of an ideal gas is enclosed in a cubical volume \(V\) labeled \(\text{ABCDEFGH}\) at temperature \(T = 300\text{ K}\). Face \(\text{EFGH}\) totally absorbs any gas molecule incident on it, while the opposite face \(\text{ABCD}\) reflects molecules elastically.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Take the normal to face \(\text{ABCD}\) and face \(\text{EFGH}\) as the \(x\)-axis. Let a gas molecule of mass \(m\) approach a wall with normal velocity component \(v_x\) directed toward the wall.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Pressure on a wall is the normal force per unit area, which equals the rate of change of normal momentum of the molecules per unit area: \(P = \frac{1}{A}\frac{\Delta p}{\Delta t}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
For an elastic collision with the reflecting face \(\text{ABCD}\), a molecule rebounds with normal velocity \(-v_x\). The magnitude of momentum change per molecule is: \[\Delta p_{\text{ABCD}} = | -m v_x - m v_x | = 2 m v_x\] For a totally absorbing collision with face \(\text{EFGH}\), the molecule comes to rest upon hitting the wall (final normal velocity is \(0\)). The magnitude of momentum change per molecule is: \[\Delta p_{\text{EFGH}} = | 0 - m v_x | = m v_x = \frac{1}{2} \Delta p_{\text{ABCD}}\] Because the number of molecules striking unit area per unit time with a given velocity is the same for both opposite faces at any given instant, the pressure on \(\text{EFGH}\) is half the pressure on \(\text{ABCD}\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Since momentum transfer per collision is halved on an absorbing wall compared to an elastically reflecting wall, the pressure on \(\text{EFGH}\) is half that on \(\text{ABCD}\).

answer.text: the pressure on \(\text{EFGH}\) would be zero.
the pressure on all the faces will be equal.
the pressure of \(\text{EFGH}\) would be double the pressure on \(\text{ABCD}\).
the pressure on \(\text{EFGH}\) would be half that on \(\text{ABCD}\).

name.text: PHYSICS_MCQI_KINETICTHEORY_MCQ_Q03 - Process for which Boyle's law applies

questiontext.text: 13.3 Boyle's law is applicable for an

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Boyle's law states that for a fixed mass (constant number of moles \(n\)) of an ideal gas at constant temperature \(T\), the pressure \(p\) of the gas is inversely proportional to its volume \(V\), so that \(pV = \text{constant}\).

Step 2: Evaluation
From the ideal gas equation \(pV = nRT\), the product \(pV\) remains constant if and only if the absolute temperature \(T\) is held constant (for a fixed \(n\)). A thermodynamic process carried out at constant temperature is called an isothermal process.

Step 3: Application
In an adiabatic process, no heat is exchanged and temperature generally changes; in an isobaric process, pressure is constant; and in an isochoric process, volume is constant. None of these generally satisfy \(pV = \text{constant}\).

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, Boyle's law is applicable for an isothermal process.

answer.text: adiabatic process.
isothermal process.
isobaric process.
isochoric process.

name.text: PHYSICS_MCQI_KINETICTHEORY_MCQ_Q04 - Heating gas in cylinder with frictionless piston

questiontext.text: 13.4 A cylinder containing an ideal gas is in vertical position and has a piston of mass \(M\) that is able to move up or down without friction (Fig. 13.2). If the temperature is increased,

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
An ideal gas is enclosed in a vertical cylinder fitted with a movable, frictionless piston of mass \(M\). The temperature \(T\) of the gas is increased.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Assume the external atmospheric pressure \(p_{\text{atm}}\) and acceleration due to gravity \(g\) are constant, and the piston has cross-sectional area \(A\). The piston moves quasi-statically so that mechanical equilibrium is maintained.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Force balance on the piston gives the gas pressure: \[p = p_{\text{atm}} + \frac{Mg}{A}\] The ideal gas law is: \[pV = nRT\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Since \(p_{\text{atm}}\), \(M\), \(g\), and \(A\) are all constant, the pressure \(p\) of the gas remains constant throughout the heating process. As the temperature \(T\) increases at constant pressure \(p\) and constant number of moles \(n\), the ideal gas equation \(V = \frac{nR}{p}T\) shows that the volume \(V\) must increase (Charles's law).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The piston rises to accommodate the expansion while keeping the pressure constant. Thus, \(V\) will change but not \(p\).

answer.text: both \(p\) and \(V\) of the gas will change.
only \(p\) will increase according to Charle's law.
\(V\) will change but not \(p\).
\(p\) will change but not \(V\).

name.text: PHYSICS_MCQI_KINETICTHEORY_MCQ_Q05 - Comparing constant pressures from V-T graphs

questiontext.text: 13.5 Volume versus temperature graphs for a given mass of an ideal gas are shown in Fig. 13.3 at two different values of constant pressure. What can be inferred about relation between \(P_{1}\) & \(P_{2}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Two straight-line graphs of volume \(V\) (in litres) versus absolute temperature \(T\) (in \(\text{K}\)) are given for a fixed mass (constant \(n\) moles) of an ideal gas at two different constant pressures \(P_1\) and \(P_2\). From the diagram, the line for \(P_2\) has a steeper slope than the line for \(P_1\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The gas obeys the ideal gas equation, and \(T\) is measured on the Kelvin scale with both lines passing through the origin.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
From the ideal gas equation \(PV = nRT\), expressing \(V\) as a function of \(T\) at constant pressure \(P\): \[V = \left(\frac{nR}{P}\right)T\] Comparing this with \(y = mx\), the slope of the \(V\)–\(T\) graph is: \[\text{Slope} = \frac{nR}{P}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Since \(n\) and \(R\) are constant, the slope is inversely proportional to the pressure: \[\text{Slope} \propto \frac{1}{P}\] From the given graph, at any fixed temperature \(T\) (for instance, \(T = 200\text{ K}\)), the volume on the \(P_2\) line is greater than the volume on the \(P_1\) line, so: \[\text{Slope}_2 > \text{Slope}_1 \implies \frac{nR}{P_2} > \frac{nR}{P_1} \implies P_1 > P_2\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
At a fixed temperature, a smaller volume corresponds to a higher pressure (\(PV = \text{constant}\)). Hence, \(P_1 > P_2\).

answer.text: data is insufficient.

name.text: PHYSICS_MCQI_KINETICTHEORY_MCQ_Q06 - Final pressure after dissociation of hydrogen

questiontext.text: 13.6 1 mole of \(\mathrm{H}_{2}\) gas is contained in a box of volume \(V = 1.00\text{ m}^3\) at \(T = 300\text{ K}\). The gas is heated to a temperature of \(T = 3000\text{ K}\) and the gas gets converted to a gas of hydrogen atoms. The final pressure would be (considering all gases to be ideal)

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initial number of moles of \(\mathrm{H}_2\) gas, \(n_1 = 1\text{ mol}\); volume of the rigid box, \(V_1 = V_2 = V = 1.00\text{ m}^3\); initial temperature, \(T_1 = 300\text{ K}\); final temperature, \(T_2 = 3000\text{ K}\). At \(3000\text{ K}\), all \(\mathrm{H}_2\) molecules dissociate into hydrogen atoms (\(\mathrm{H}\)).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Both molecular hydrogen and atomic hydrogen behave as ideal gases, and the container volume remains constant.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
Ideal gas equation: \[pV = nRT \implies p = \frac{nRT}{V}\] Dissociation reaction: \[\mathrm{H}_2 \rightarrow 2\mathrm{H}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
From the dissociation reaction, \(1\text{ mole}\) of \(\mathrm{H}_2\) produces \(2\text{ moles}\) of \(\mathrm{H}\) atoms, so \(n_2 = 2\text{ mol}\). The initial pressure is: \[p_1 = \frac{n_1 R T_1}{V} = \frac{1 \times R \times 300}{V}\] The final pressure is: \[p_2 = \frac{n_2 R T_2}{V} = \frac{2 \times R \times 3000}{V}\] Taking the ratio of final to initial pressure: \[\frac{p_2}{p_1} = \left(\frac{n_2}{n_1}\right)\left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right) = \left(\frac{2}{1}\right)\left(\frac{3000}{300}\right) = 2 \times 10 = 20\] Thus, \(p_2 = 20\,p_1\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The number of moles doubles and the absolute temperature increases by a factor of \(10\) at constant volume, so the pressure increases by \(2 \times 10 = 20\) times. The final pressure would be \(20\) times the pressure initially.

answer.text: same as the pressure initially.
2 times the pressure initially.
10 times the pressure initially.
20 times the pressure initially.

name.text: PHYSICS_MCQI_KINETICTHEORY_MCQ_Q07 - Speed distribution of hydrogen and oxygen mixture

questiontext.text: 13.7 A vessel of volume \(V\) contains a mixture of 1 mole of Hydrogen and 1 mole of Oxygen (both considered as ideal). Let \(f_{1}(v)dv\), denote the fraction of molecules with speed between \(v\) and \((v + dv)\) with \(f_{2}(v)dv\), similarly for oxygen. Then

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
According to the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution law, for an ideal gas in thermal equilibrium at absolute temperature \(T\), the fraction of molecules having speeds in the range \(v\) to \(v + dv\) is: \[f(v)\,dv = 4\pi \left(\frac{m}{2\pi k_B T}\right)^{3/2} v^2 e^{-\frac{mv^2}{2k_B T}}\,dv\] where \(m\) is the mass of a single molecule of that gas and \(k_B\) is Boltzmann's constant.

Step 2: Evaluation
In a mixture of non-reacting ideal gases in thermal equilibrium, both hydrogen and oxygen are at the same temperature \(T\), and each species independently obeys the Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution corresponding to its own molecular mass \(m_1\) (for hydrogen) and \(m_2\) (for oxygen).

Step 3: Application
Because \(m_1 \neq m_2\), the functions \(f_1(v)\) and \(f_2(v)\) are not identical. Furthermore, their sum \(f_1(v) + f_2(v)\) is not a single Maxwell distribution for a single molecular mass (and its integral over all speeds would be \(2\) rather than \(1\)). Instead, \(f_1(v)\) and \(f_2(v)\) each obey Maxwell's distribution law separately.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
Therefore, \(f_1(v)\) and \(f_2(v)\) will obey the Maxwell's distribution law separately.

answer.text: \(f_{1}(v) + f_{2}(v) = f(v)\) obeys the Maxwell's distribution law.
\(f_{1}(v), f_{2}(v)\) will obey the Maxwell's distribution law separately.
Neither \(f_{1}(v)\), nor \(f_{2}(v)\) will obey the Maxwell's distribution law.
\(f_{2}(v)\) and \(f_{1}(v)\) will be the same.

name.text: PHYSICS_MCQI_KINETICTHEORY_MCQ_Q08 - Final pressure of gas in heated balloon

questiontext.text: 13.8 An inflated rubber balloon contains one mole of an ideal gas, has a pressure \(p\), volume \(V\) and temperature \(T\). If the temperature rises to \(1.1\,T\), and the volume is increased to \(1.05\,V\), the final pressure will be

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Number of moles of the ideal gas, \(n = 1\text{ mol}\) (constant). Initial state: pressure \(p_1 = p\), volume \(V_1 = V\), temperature \(T_1 = T\). Final state: temperature \(T_2 = 1.1\,T\), volume \(V_2 = 1.05\,V\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The gas is ideal and no gas leaks out of the balloon, so \(n\) remains constant.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
From the ideal gas equation \(pV = nRT\), for a fixed amount of gas: \[\frac{p_1 V_1}{T_1} = \frac{p_2 V_2}{T_2}\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Solving for the final pressure \(p_2\): \[p_2 = p_1 \left(\frac{T_2}{T_1}\right)\left(\frac{V_1}{V_2}\right) = p \left(\frac{1.1\,T}{T}\right)\left(\frac{V}{1.05\,V}\right) = p \left(\frac{1.1}{1.05}\right) \approx 1.0476\,p\] Since \(1 < 1.0476 < 1.1\), the final pressure \(p_2\) satisfies \(p < p_2 < 1.1\,p\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Temperature increases by \(10\%\) while volume increases by \(5\%\), so the net pressure increase is slightly less than \(5\%\). Therefore, the final pressure will be between \(p\) and \(1.1\,p\).

answer.text: less than \(p\)
between \(p\) and \(1.1\).

name.text: PHYSICS_MCQII_KINETICTHEORY_MCQ_Q09 - Kinetic theory pressure for ionized hydrogen

questiontext.text:
13.9 \(\text{ABCDEFGH}\) is a hollow cube made of an insulator (Fig. 13.4). Face \(\text{ABCD}\) has positive charge on it. Inside the cube, we have ionized hydrogen.

The usual kinetic theory expression for pressure

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The standard kinetic theory expression for pressure \(p = \frac{1}{3}\rho v_{\text{rms}}^2\) is derived under the assumptions that gas molecules experience no forces except during brief, elastic collisions with the walls (and other molecules), and that the velocity distribution is isotropic (\(\overline{v_x^2} = \overline{v_y^2} = \overline{v_z^2} = \frac{1}{3}v_{\text{rms}}^2\)).

Step 2: Evaluation
Inside the insulating cube, ionized hydrogen consists of positively charged protons and negatively charged electrons. Because face \(\text{ABCD}\) carries a positive charge, it produces an electric field inside the cube directed away from \(\text{ABCD}\).

Step 3: Application
Due to this electric field, the ions experience continuous electrostatic forces in addition to forces during collisions with the walls, violating the assumption of force-free motion between collisions. Furthermore, the electric field introduces a preferred direction perpendicular to face \(\text{ABCD}\), so the motion and spatial distribution of the charged particles are no longer isotropic—isotropy is lost. Collisions with the insulating walls, however, can still be treated as elastic, so inelastic wall collisions are not the reason for invalidity.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The usual kinetic theory expression for pressure will not be valid because the ions experience forces other than those due to collisions with the walls, and because isotropy is lost.

answer.text: will be valid.
will not be valid since the ions would experience forces other than due to collisions with the walls.
will not be valid since collisions with walls would not be elastic.
will not be valid because isotropy is lost.

name.text: PHYSICS_MCQII_KINETICTHEORY_MCQ_Q10 - Meaning of energy in kinetic theory equation

questiontext.text: 13.10 Diatomic molecules like hydrogen have energies due to both translational as well as rotational motion. From the equation in kinetic theory \(pV = \frac{2}{3} E\), \(E\) is

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In the kinetic theory of gases, pressure on the container walls is calculated from the rate of change of linear momentum of the molecules colliding normally with the walls: \[p = \frac{1}{3}\frac{Nm}{V}\overline{v^2} = \frac{2}{3V}\left(\frac{1}{2}Nm\overline{v^2}\right)\] where \(N\) is the total number of molecules of mass \(m\) and \(\overline{v^2}\) is the mean square translational speed.

Step 2: Evaluation
Multiplying both sides by volume \(V\) gives \(pV = \frac{2}{3}E\), where \(E = \frac{1}{2}Nm\overline{v^2}\) is the total translational kinetic energy of all the molecules in the volume \(V\) (not energy per unit volume).

Step 3: Application
Even though diatomic molecules also possess rotational kinetic energy (which is \(\frac{2}{3}\) of the translational kinetic energy on average, so not negligible, and always non-negative), rotational motion does not contribute to the change in linear momentum during collisions with the walls and therefore does not contribute to the gas pressure.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
In the equation \(pV = \frac{2}{3}E\), \(E\) represents only the translational part of the energy because during collisions with the wall, pressure relates to the change in linear momentum.

answer.text: the total energy per unit volume.
only the translational part of energy because rotational energy is very small compared to the translational energy.
only the translational part of the energy because during collisions with the wall pressure relates to change in linear momentum.
the translational part of the energy because rotational energies of molecules can be of either sign and its average over all the molecules is zero.

name.text: PHYSICS_MCQII_KINETICTHEORY_MCQ_Q11 - Rotational energy of a diatomic gas molecule

questiontext.text: 13.11 In a diatomic molecule, the rotational energy at a given temperature

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
For a diatomic gas molecule in thermal equilibrium at absolute temperature \(T\), the total energy (neglecting vibration) consists of \(3\) translational degrees of freedom and \(2\) rotational degrees of freedom, each appearing as a quadratic term in the energy expression: \[\varepsilon = \frac{1}{2}m v_x^2 + \frac{1}{2}m v_y^2 + \frac{1}{2}m v_z^2 + \frac{1}{2}I_1 \omega_1^2 + \frac{1}{2}I_2 \omega_2^2\]

Step 2: Evaluation
Because each rotational degree of freedom is quadratic in angular velocity just as each translational degree of freedom is quadratic in linear velocity, the rotational energy obeys the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution at a given temperature \(T\). Consequently, different molecules have different rotational energies rather than the same fixed value.

Step 3: Application
By the law of equipartition of energy, each quadratic degree of freedom carries an average energy of \(\frac{1}{2}k_B T\). Thus, the average rotational kinetic energy (for \(2\) degrees of freedom) is \(2 \times \frac{1}{2}k_B T = k_B T\), while the average translational kinetic energy (for \(3\) degrees of freedom) is \(3 \times \frac{1}{2}k_B T = \frac{3}{2}k_B T\). Comparing the two gives: \[\frac{\langle E_{\text{rot}} \rangle}{\langle E_{\text{trans}} \rangle} = \frac{k_B T}{\frac{3}{2}k_B T} = \frac{2}{3}\]

Step 4: Final Conclusion
In a diatomic molecule, the rotational energy at a given temperature obeys Maxwell's distribution and is \(\frac{2}{3}\)rd the translational kinetic energy.

answer.text: obeys Maxwell's distribution.
have the same value for all molecules.
equals the translational kinetic energy for each molecule.
is (2/3)rd the translational kinetic energy for each molecule.

name.text: PHYSICS_MCQII_KINETICTHEORY_MCQ_Q12 - Graphs depicting ideal gas behaviour

questiontext.text: 13.12 Which of the following diagrams (Fig. 13.5) depicts ideal gas behaviour?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Four thermodynamic plots are presented: a \(V\) versus \(T\) plot at constant \(P\), a \(P\) versus \(V\) plot at constant \(T\), a \(P\) versus \(T\) plot at constant \(V\), and a \(PV\) versus \(T\) plot.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
An ideal gas of fixed number of moles \(n\) obeys \(PV = nRT\), where \(T\) is the absolute temperature in Kelvin.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. At constant \(P\): \(V = \left(\frac{nR}{P}\right)T\), a straight line passing through the origin.
2. At constant \(T\): \(PV = \text{constant}\), a rectangular hyperbola.
3. At constant \(V\): \(P = \left(\frac{nR}{V}\right)T\), a straight line passing through the origin.
4. In general: \(PV = nRT\), so \(PV\) is directly proportional to \(T\), forming a straight line through the origin with positive slope \(nR\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Evaluating each plot against the ideal gas equation:
- The \(V\) versus \(T\) plot at constant \(P\) is shown as a straight line passing through the origin, which correctly represents Charles's law.
- The \(P\) versus \(V\) plot at constant \(T\) is shown as a straight line with negative slope instead of a rectangular hyperbola, so it does not depict ideal gas behaviour.
- The \(P\) versus \(T\) plot at constant \(V\) is shown as a straight line passing through the origin, which correctly represents Gay-Lussac's law.
- The \(PV\) versus \(T\) plot is shown as a horizontal line independent of \(T\), whereas \(PV = nRT\) requires \(PV\) to increase linearly with \(T\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Only the \(V\)–\(T\) graph at constant \(P\) and the \(P\)–\(T\) graph at constant \(V\) correctly depict ideal gas behaviour.

name.text: PHYSICS_MCQII_KINETICTHEORY_MCQ_Q13 - Increase in kinetic energy during adiabatic compression

questiontext.text: 13.13 When an ideal gas is compressed adiabatically, its temperature rises: the molecules on the average have more kinetic energy than before. The kinetic energy increases,

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In an adiabatic compression, no heat enters or leaves the system (\(\Delta Q = 0\)). By the first law of thermodynamics, the work done on the gas by the external agent increases its internal energy (\(\Delta U = -\Delta W > 0\)), which raises the temperature and average kinetic energy of the molecules.

Step 2: Evaluation
Microscopically, when a piston (a moving part of the wall) moves inward with speed \(u\), a gas molecule approaching it with normal speed \(v\) rebounds elastically with speed \(v + 2u\), thereby gaining kinetic energy. In contrast, collisions with stationary walls do no work and leave the molecular speed unchanged.

Step 3: Application
Ideal gas molecules experience no forces inside the volume between collisions, so they are not accelerated within the interior volume. Similarly, intermolecular collisions merely redistribute energy among molecules while conserving the total kinetic energy, so redistribution cannot increase the average kinetic energy.

Step 4: Final Conclusion
The average kinetic energy of the molecules increases solely because of collisions with the moving parts of the wall.

answer.text: because of collisions with moving parts of the wall only.
because of collisions with the entire wall.
because the molecules gets accelerated in their motion inside the volume.
because of redistribution of energy amongst the molecules.
